paragraphs: A population of cortical neurons responds to sensory input while also being influenced by internal states that change over different timescales. This paper develops a statistical model for separating those influences in recordings of neural spikes. Its aim is to recover an organized hierarchy of population states and describe how those states affect responses to sensory input.

The model combines a hidden Markov decision tree with a generalized linear observation model. The tree represents the hierarchy of unobserved states, while state-dependent tuning parameters allow neural responses to vary with the current state. A variational Bayesian algorithm estimates a posterior distribution over the model parameters from recordings, rather than treating their values as known.

On simulated data, the method recovers state sequences and reconstructs the underlying parameters. In visual cortex recordings, a model with two hierarchical levels outperforms both one-state and two-state generalized linear models. Accounting for state dependence also improves sensory decoding, suggesting that internal population states contain information relevant to interpreting neural responses.
neurips-2014-a-bayesian-model-for-identi.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian model recovers internal neural population states and improves sensory decoding by accounting for state-dependent responses.

paragraphs: Sparse logistic regression combines classification with feature selection by using an l1 penalty that makes some fitted coefficients zero. With very many candidate features, solving the optimization problem can still be expensive. This paper introduces Slores, a screening rule that identifies coefficients that will be zero so their corresponding features can be excluded from the optimization.

The practical value is in reducing the problem before the main solver does its work. Screening requires only one scan of the dataset, and the authors describe its cost as negligible compared with solving sparse logistic regression. Because the rule is independent of the optimization solver, it can be combined with existing solvers rather than requiring a replacement.

Experiments use high-dimensional datasets from several applications. The authors report better screening performance than existing state-of-the-art rules and roughly an order-of-magnitude improvement in solving efficiency in general. These are empirical results; the potential reduction in feature count depends on how many zero coefficients the rule can identify in a given problem.
neurips-2014-a-safe-screening-rule-for-s.tldr: Slores speeds up sparse logistic regression by screening out features whose fitted coefficients will be zero.

paragraphs: Object categorization needs representations that distinguish categories, but a useful representation can also express what categories mean. This paper learns a shared space containing object categories, broader supercategories, and attributes. Placing these semantic entities directly in the category space allows the model to describe a category through a linear combination of meaningful components.

The method encourages each category to use a sparse combination of a supercategory and attributes. Sparsity keeps the description compact by limiting the components involved. An additional exclusive regularization term encourages compositions that discriminate between categories. The semantic reconstruction requirement therefore participates in learning the representation, rather than serving only as extra information supplied alongside it.

The authors state that this reconstructive regularization guides discriminative learning toward better generalization. It also produces compact semantic descriptions that people can inspect to understand what the model has learned. The contribution connects predictive usefulness with interpretability: category distinctions and their semantic explanations are developed within the same representation.
neurips-2014-a-unified-semantic-embeddin.tldr: A shared embedding represents object categories as sparse combinations of supercategories and attributes, supporting discrimination and interpretable descriptions.

paragraphs: Estimating human pose from a single image requires identifying body parts and determining how they fit together. This paper uses local image evidence for both tasks. Its graphical model allows relationships between pairs of parts to depend on the image, so the evidence informs the expected arrangement as well as the presence of individual joints.

A mixture model represents the possible spatial relationships between parts. Deep convolutional neural networks learn conditional probabilities for part presence and spatial relationships within image patches. These predictions feed into the graphical representation of pose. The combination brings learned local visual information into a model that explicitly represents connections among the body's parts.

The authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods on the LSP and FLIC datasets. They also report strong performance on Buffy without training on that dataset. The findings support the usefulness of predicting relationships from image content, alongside detecting parts, within the evaluated pose-estimation tasks.
neurips-2014-articulated-pose-estimation.tldr: A pose-estimation model uses convolutional networks to predict both body parts and image-dependent spatial relationships between them.

paragraphs: Optimization over permutations can be approached by replacing discrete choices with a continuous convex set. A common representation uses the Birkhoff polytope, the convex hull of permutation matrices, and requires a quadratic number of variables and constraints. This paper investigates a more compact representation when the relevant objects are permutation vectors.

The authors use a construction for the permutahedron, the convex hull of those vectors. It reduces the representation size to Θ(n log n) in theory and Θ(n log² n) in practice. They adapt an existing convex formulation of the 2-SUM problem to use this smaller polytope, making the representation itself the source of computational savings.

For large problems, the adapted formulation produces results of similar quality in substantially less computation time. The paper also introduces a simpler regularization scheme with good empirical results. The scope matters: the compact formulation concerns optimization over permutation vectors, and the demonstrated computational benefits come from applying it to the stated 2-SUM formulation.
neurips-2014-beyond-the-birkhoff-polytop.tldr: A compact permutahedron formulation reduces the size of vector-permutation relaxations and accelerates a convex 2-SUM method while preserving similar solution quality.

paragraphs: Optimization methods can benefit from measuring changes in a way that reflects a problem's structure. Mirror descent does this by replacing squared Euclidean distance with a Bregman divergence. This paper applies a similar generalization to the alternating direction method of multipliers, introducing Bregman ADMM, or BADMM, with a choice of divergences.

The resulting framework encompasses ADMM and several variants, including generalized, inexact, and Bethe ADMM. The authors establish global convergence and an O(1/T) iteration complexity. These results give theoretical support to the generalized method while allowing different divergences to exploit different problem structures. The abstract also states that, in some cases, BADMM can be faster by a factor of O(n/ln n).

For the mass transportation linear program, the method permits extensive parallel computation and straightforward GPU execution. The authors report performance several times faster than Gurobi in that application. The speed claims therefore include both a qualified theoretical advantage and a concrete application result, rather than a universal improvement for every optimization problem.
neurips-2014-bregman-alternating-directi.tldr: BADMM generalizes ADMM with Bregman divergences, providing convergence guarantees and substantial speed improvements in the reported transportation application.

paragraphs: The Kikuchi approximation provides a way to estimate a log partition function using a region graph. This paper studies a reweighted version, asking which assignments of weights make its objective concave. Concavity matters because it gives the approximate optimization problem a structure that supports guarantees about the quality of an optimizer.

The authors establish sufficient conditions on the weights. They also show that a reweighted sum-product algorithm produces a global optimum of the Kikuchi approximation whenever it converges. Both qualifications matter: the result concerns the approximate objective, and the conclusion is conditional on convergence. It does not assert that every run must converge.

For region graphs with two layers, corresponding to the Bethe approximation, the weight conditions are necessary as well as sufficient. The paper further characterizes the polytope of concavity through the graph's cycle structure. Simulations demonstrate advantages of the reweighted approach, connecting these structural results to observed inference performance.
neurips-2014-concavity-of-reweighted-kik.tldr: The paper identifies weights that make reweighted Kikuchi objectives concave and establishes global optimality of the approximation when its message-passing algorithm converges.

paragraphs: Article recommendations can draw on both reading histories and the contents of articles. This paper develops collaborative topic Poisson factorization, or CTPF, to connect those sources in a generative model. It learns representations of articles and reader preferences together, using them to recommend articles suited to individual readers.

CTPF uses Poisson distributions to model reader behavior and article text. Latent topics describing the text are connected to latent preferences describing readers. This shared representation supports personalized prediction and offers an interpretable view of readership patterns. The model's internal space therefore serves both recommendation and analysis of how reading preferences relate to content.

The authors use stochastic variational inference to fit the model to large datasets. They report fitting the full arXiv usage dataset, with more than 43 million ratings and 42 million word counts, within a day. Their empirical comparisons show better recommendations than several baselines, including the previous state-of-the-art approach, alongside evidence that the model can operate at substantial scale.
neurips-2014-content-based-recommendatio.tldr: CTPF connects article topics with reader preferences in a scalable Poisson model that improves recommendations in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Hippocampal place fields reflect more than physical position: their patterns can depend on travel direction, rewards, and environmental geometry. This paper proposes that a cognitive map represents predictions about future locations under the current pattern of movement. That hypothesis links the representation of space to the behavior it needs to support.

Under the proposed model, rewards, barriers, and directional preferences influence transitions through space and thereby shape place fields. Several observed place-field phenomena arise naturally from this organization. The authors also demonstrate that the representation can support efficient reinforcement learning, connecting their account of neural activity with a computational role in learning to navigate.

The paper additionally proposes that grid cells compute an eigendecomposition of place fields that helps divide an enclosure along natural boundaries. Repeating this segmentation can produce a hierarchy of spatial regions. This motivates the possibility that grid cells help compute subgoals for hierarchical reinforcement learning; the abstract presents that biological role as a proposal, rather than an established fact.
neurips-2014-design-principles-of-the-hi.tldr: The paper proposes that place fields predict future locations and that grid cells may help organize spatial subgoals for navigation.

paragraphs: A video summary needs useful content without excessive repetition, and the order of events matters. This paper treats summarization as supervised subset selection. Human-created summaries provide examples from which the system learns to choose informative, diverse content, with evaluation tied to measures derived from how people perceive summary quality.

The proposed sequential determinantal point process, or seqDPP, is a probabilistic model for selecting diverse subsets from sequences. A standard determinantal point process can represent diversity, but it treats frames as items whose order can be freely rearranged. SeqDPP incorporates the sequential structure of video while retaining the ability to favor diverse selections.

Experiments on three video datasets show better performance than existing unsupervised methods and naive uses of the standard DPP model. These comparisons support the combined value of learning from human summaries and respecting temporal structure. The contribution is thus a selection model in which diversity and sequence information can both influence the resulting summary.
neurips-2014-diverse-sequential-subset-s.tldr: SeqDPP learns from human summaries to select diverse video content while respecting its sequential structure.

paragraphs: If neural circuits represent uncertainty by generating samples, inference quality depends on how quickly they produce new samples that are not strongly correlated with earlier ones. This paper studies that speed bottleneck in a linear-Gaussian latent variable model, where stochastic neural networks with linear dynamics can sample from the posterior distribution.

The authors show analytically and through simulations that Langevin sampling's symmetric synaptic weights cause critically slow mixing for high-dimensional posteriors. They then use control theory to construct networks that are optimally fast within the studied framework. These networks are reported to be orders of magnitude faster than Langevin sampling and more biologically plausible.

The faster networks briefly amplify selected components of external noise, producing the spatial correlations required by the posterior. They dynamically maintain a balance between excitation and inhibition while violating detailed balance in their sampling transitions. The result distinguishes two meanings of balance and illustrates how statistically irreversible dynamics can accelerate sampling in this specific neural model.
neurips-2014-fast-sampling-based-inferen.tldr: In a linear-Gaussian model, balanced neural networks with irreversible sampling dynamics generate posterior samples much faster than Langevin sampling.

paragraphs: Large datasets often make it useful to cluster observations incrementally, processing one item at a time and retaining only a small portion of the data. This paper asks what kinds of cluster structure such methods can identify. Its focus is on the capabilities of the incremental setting itself, rather than only the performance of one particular algorithm.

The authors prove that the incremental model is strictly weaker than the batch model they study. They identify a fundamental class of cluster structures that can be recovered in the batch setting but cannot be identified by any incremental method in their setting. This establishes a structural obstacle that cannot simply be resolved by choosing a better incremental algorithm.

The paper then shows that permitting additional clusters can overcome the identified limitations. The number of clusters is therefore an important part of the comparison between incremental and batch processing. Allowing more clusters changes what incremental methods can recover, providing a theoretical reason to consider extra clusters when moving from batch analysis to incremental processing.
neurips-2014-incremental-clustering-the-.tldr: The paper proves a gap between incremental and batch clustering and shows that allowing extra clusters can overcome the identified limitations.

paragraphs: L-BFGS is used to estimate parameters in machine learning, but distributing it across very large clusters creates computational difficulties. This paper studies clusters containing tens of thousands of independent commodity machines. It shows that a straightforward MapReduce implementation requires either substantial memory or many MapReduce stages, both of which can hurt performance.

The proposed Vector-free L-BFGS reorganizes the algorithm to avoid expensive dot-product operations in its two-loop recursion. This creates more opportunity for parallel execution and improves computational efficiency. The authors prove mathematical equivalence with L-BFGS, so the contribution concerns how the computation is organized while retaining the underlying algorithm's mathematical behavior.

Experiments on real-world machine learning problems in production clusters demonstrate strong performance and scalability with billions of variables. The findings connect a specific computational bottleneck to the ability to train much larger models. They show that reformulating the internal operations of an established optimizer can make it substantially better suited to distributed infrastructure.
neurips-2014-large-scale-l-bfgs-using-ma.tldr: Vector-free L-BFGS preserves mathematical equivalence while reorganizing costly operations for scalable MapReduce optimization with billions of variables.

paragraphs: Document collections can contain both recurring word patterns and human-assigned labels, but the two sources of organization do not necessarily align neatly. Labels may be numerous, noisy, or missing. This paper introduces Label to Hierarchy, or L2H, to learn a hierarchy of user-generated labels together with topics associated with those labels.

The input consists of documents that can each have multiple labels. The model combines their textual structure with those annotations, accounting for missing labels supplied by different, untrained annotators. Organizing labels hierarchically provides an interpretable summary of a label collection that would otherwise be difficult to understand as a large flat set.

The authors evaluate the model by predicting held-out words and labels for previously unseen documents and report empirical effectiveness on both tasks. These evaluations connect the learned organization to predictive usefulness as well as interpretability. The result is a model that relates document content and imperfect annotations through a jointly learned conceptual hierarchy.
neurips-2014-learning-a-concept-hierarch.tldr: L2H learns an interpretable hierarchy of document labels and associated topics while accounting for missing human annotations.

paragraphs: Algorithms for prediction with expert advice use a learning rate to control how aggressively they respond to observed performance. Existing theoretical choices for exponential weights can be more conservative than choices that work well empirically. This paper addresses that gap by learning the learning rate over a broad range of possible values.

The method competes with the empirically best learning rate in that range, including both small values and values much larger than those covered by earlier formal guarantees. Its performance matches that reference up to a factor that is at most polylogarithmic in the number of experts and the inverse learning rate. The claim is approximate competitiveness, rather than exact equality.

Although the approach uses a grid of learning rates, it runs in linear time regardless of the grid's size. This makes considering many candidate rates computationally attractive. The contribution combines adaptation to empirical performance with a theoretical guarantee, extending the range of aggressive learning behavior that can be supported by analysis.
neurips-2014-learning-the-learning-rate-.tldr: The method learns a learning rate that competes with the empirically best choice across a broad grid while retaining linear runtime.

paragraphs: A graphical model's partition function is the normalizing constant needed to turn its scores into probabilities. Computing it for a general pairwise binary graphical model is NP-hard, motivating approximate inference. This paper addresses a tradeoff between two established methods: belief propagation often gives reasonable estimates but has convergence problems, while tree-reweighted belief propagation converges better but typically estimates less accurately.

The authors construct a particular attractive 2-cover from an arbitrary pairwise binary graphical model. They analyze properties of this auxiliary construction and use it to build an estimation algorithm. The construction is the central technical device for obtaining a different balance between convergence behavior and partition-function estimation quality.

The resulting scheme has better convergence properties than belief propagation. It also provably improves on tree-reweighted belief propagation's partition-function estimates in many instances. That qualification is central: the abstract establishes an advantage across many cases, rather than claiming uniformly superior estimates for every possible model. The contribution combines an algorithmic construction with guarantees about this tradeoff.
neurips-2014-making-pairwise-binary-grap.tldr: An attractive 2-cover construction improves convergence over belief propagation and provably improves partition-function estimates over tree-reweighted belief propagation in many instances.

paragraphs: Learning prices becomes more complicated when buyers behave strategically in response to a seller's algorithm. This paper studies revenue learning for posted-price auctions through strategic regret. It first examines a broad family of monotone regret-minimization algorithms, including the previously best-known method, to determine what performance that family can achieve.

The authors prove that no algorithm in this monotone family can achieve strategic regret better than an Ω(√T) lower bound. They then introduce a new algorithm whose strategic regret lies within an O(log T) factor of a lower bound, reporting an exponential improvement over the previous best algorithm. The family-specific impossibility result is distinct from the near-optimality claim for the new method.

The paper also emphasizes a natural analysis and simpler proofs for its algorithm, with design ideas described as general. Empirical comparisons against the previous best algorithm show consistent exponential improvement in several scenarios. Together, the results identify a limitation of an existing algorithm family and demonstrate a substantially stronger approach to the strategic pricing problem.
neurips-2014-optimal-regret-minimization.tldr: The paper proves limits for monotone strategic-pricing algorithms and introduces a new method with regret close to a lower bound.

paragraphs: Many convex optimization problems have an objective split into blocks, with linear constraints connecting those blocks. ADMM is well studied for two-block problems, but extending its effectiveness to multiple blocks is less straightforward. This paper introduces the Parallel Direction Method of Multipliers, or PDMM, for this multi-block setting.

PDMM randomly selects some blocks and updates them in parallel, giving it a structure similar to parallel randomized block coordinate descent. The authors establish global convergence and iteration complexity with a constant step size. They also show that the method can perform randomized block coordinate descent on overlapping blocks, extending the types of block organization it can handle.

Experiments cover robust principal component analysis and overlapping group lasso. In these two applications, PDMM performs better than the compared state-of-the-art methods. The contribution combines a way to coordinate parallel block updates under linear constraints with theoretical support and application results. Its stated setting remains convex, block-separable objectives with the specified constraint structure.
neurips-2014-parallel-direction-method-o.tldr: PDMM solves multi-block constrained convex problems through randomized parallel updates with convergence guarantees and favorable results in two applications.

paragraphs: Submodular maximization appears in many machine learning problems, but moving effective serial algorithms into parallel execution can be difficult. This paper focuses on non-monotone objectives, the more general setting in which adding an item need not improve the objective. It develops two ways to parallelize the strongly sequential double-greedy algorithm.

The first method removes coordination to emphasize speed, accepting a weaker approximation guarantee. The second uses concurrency control and preserves a tight one-half approximation guarantee, at a quantifiable cost in coordination and available parallelism. These alternatives make explicit the relationship between execution speed and the strength of guaranteed solution quality.

The authors implement both methods on multicore hardware and evaluate them using graphs with a billion edges. The results demonstrate scalability and the practical tradeoffs of the two designs. The central contribution is therefore both algorithmic and comparative: it provides parallel methods while showing why maintaining a stronger optimization guarantee can require more coordination among concurrent operations.
neurips-2014-parallel-double-greedy-subm.tldr: Two parallel double-greedy methods expose the tradeoff between faster coordination-free execution and preserving a tight one-half approximation guarantee.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization must choose where to evaluate a black-box function next. Predictive Entropy Search, or PES, makes that choice by asking which evaluation is expected to reveal the most information about the global maximum. This directs evaluation toward reducing uncertainty relevant to the optimization goal.

The information-based acquisition function is intractable in its original form. PES rewrites it using the expected reduction in the differential entropy of a predictive distribution. This reformulation enables approximations that the authors describe as more accurate and efficient than alternatives such as Entropy Search. It also readily supports a fully Bayesian treatment of model hyperparameters, which the abstract contrasts with Entropy Search.

The paper evaluates PES on synthetic problems and applications in machine learning, finance, biotechnology, and robotics. The authors report significant optimization gains resulting from the increased accuracy of PES. The findings support the practical value of reformulating the information calculation: a more workable approximation to the selection rule leads to better optimization in the reported evaluations.
neurips-2014-predictive-entropy-search-f.tldr: PES reformulates information gain about a function's global maximum into a predictive-entropy calculation that improves Bayesian optimization in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: In repeated pricing, a buyer's response can depend on both the current offer and the prices that response might induce later. Motivated by advertising exchanges, this paper studies posted-price auctions where the item being sold has a context vector. A buyer's valuation is assumed to be a function of that description.

The analysis considers truthful buyers who decide myopically each round and surplus-maximizing buyers who can act strategically. A strategic buyer may give up an immediate benefit to influence the seller into offering better prices in the future. This makes observed purchasing behavior part of an interaction with the learning algorithm, complicating the task of learning prices from responses.

The authors provide an algorithm with O(T^{2/3}) regret against a surplus-maximizing buyer in the contextual setting. This sublinear bound means that regret per round decreases as the number of rounds grows. They also extend the result to repeated second-price auctions with multiple buyers, broadening the auction setting covered by the analysis.
neurips-2014-repeated-contextual-auction.tldr: The paper achieves sublinear regret for contextual pricing against a strategic buyer and extends the result to repeated second-price auctions.

paragraphs: Large datasets often contain far more examples than reliable labels, making it important to learn from labeled and unlabeled observations together. This paper revisits generative modeling for semi-supervised learning. It develops models intended to generalize effectively from a small labeled collection to a much larger unlabeled one.

The approach combines deep generative models with approximate Bayesian inference based on variational methods. These are the two central ingredients: a flexible model of the data and a practical way to perform inference in that model. The paper positions their combination as a response to earlier generative approaches that were limited by inflexibility, inefficient computation, or difficulty scaling.

The authors report significant improvements that make generative approaches highly competitive for semi-supervised learning. The stated contribution is therefore about making this modeling strategy effective and computationally practical in the scarce-label setting. It connects advances in model representation and inference to the same goal: learning usefully when obtaining labels is much harder than collecting data.
neurips-2014-semi-supervised-learning-wi.tldr: Deep generative models combined with variational Bayesian inference make generative semi-supervised learning competitive when labeled data are scarce.

paragraphs: Crowdsourcing combines labels from workers who may make mistakes, so recovering the underlying labels requires accounting for noisy responses. The Dawid-Skene estimator is widely used for this task, but its non-convex likelihood makes performance difficult to justify theoretically. This paper develops an efficient two-stage algorithm for problems with multiple possible classes.

The first stage uses a spectral method to estimate the model parameters. The second refines that estimate by applying expectation-maximization to the Dawid-Skene objective. This division gives initialization an explicit role in the overall procedure: the algorithm begins with a spectral estimate and then uses likelihood optimization to improve it.

The authors prove that the combined algorithm achieves an optimal convergence rate up to a logarithmic factor. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show accuracy comparable to the strongest empirical approach considered, while outperforming several other recent methods. The paper thus joins a near-optimal theoretical rate with competitive observed performance, without claiming to surpass the most accurate comparator.
neurips-2014-spectral-methods-meet-em-a-.tldr: Spectral initialization followed by EM yields a crowdsourcing estimator with a near-optimal convergence rate and competitive empirical accuracy.

paragraphs: Stochastic variational inference makes Bayesian analysis practical for large datasets, but its usual setting treats observations as independent or exchangeable. Hidden Markov models describe sequences with dependencies across time. This paper develops an SVI algorithm for learning their parameters while addressing the complications created by splitting a dependent sequence into minibatches.

Breaking the chain creates boundary effects because observations near a minibatch edge are separated from part of their surrounding sequence. The proposed algorithm uses the chain's memory decay to adaptively bound the errors introduced by those edges. This directly connects the stochastic approximation to the sequence's dependence structure, rather than simply treating sampled observations as independent.

The authors demonstrate the method on synthetic experiments and a large genomics dataset for which a batch algorithm is computationally infeasible. These results support its usefulness for large sequential datasets. The contribution is a way to extend minibatch-based Bayesian learning to HMMs while explicitly controlling errors caused by cutting the chain.
neurips-2014-stochastic-variational-infe.tldr: An SVI algorithm learns hidden Markov models from minibatches by using memory decay to bound errors at sequence boundaries.

paragraphs: Graph clustering can be formulated as dividing a graph into groups while balancing their sizes through a cut criterion. Spectral clustering offers a familiar relaxation, but methods for producing multiple clusters often rely on greedy choices or heuristics with a weak connection to the original objective. This paper proposes a tight continuous relaxation for any balanced k-cut problem.

The authors also analyze a related recent relaxation and show that it is loose in most cases, connecting that looseness to poor practical performance. To optimize their own formulation, they develop an algorithm for the difficult sum-of-ratios objective. The algorithm guarantees monotonic descent, meaning successive steps do not increase the objective; this is distinct from a guarantee of globally solving the optimization problem.

Extensive comparisons show the proposed method outperforming the existing approaches evaluated for ratio cut and other balanced k-cut criteria. The contribution combines a closer continuous formulation of the clustering objective with an optimization procedure that makes consistent downward progress.
neurips-2014-tight-continuous-relaxation.tldr: A tight relaxation of balanced k-cut, paired with a monotonic-descent optimizer, improves graph clustering in the reported comparisons.
